When I’m walking around campus, I catch myself checking every guy I pass, and even photos of actors online, comparing my face to theirs. I’ll zoom in on pictures and study how symmetrical they look and then go back to my own photos and pick apart all the differences. It makes it really hard to focus in lectures because I’m thinking about how weird my face must look from different angles, like people can see something wrong that I can’t quite prove but I’m sure is there. D017-D005_h024.question:
It’s mostly my face that bothers me, especially my nose and my eyes. When I look in the mirror, my nose seems twisted, like it’s leaning to one side, and my eyes look uneven, like one is drooping. My daughter and the grandkids all tell me they look “completely normal,” but I feel like they’re just being kind. I ask them about it a lot, probably every time they visit or call. I’ll say, “Are you sure my nose doesn’t look strange? Do my eyes look off?” Sometimes I even ask the pharmacist or the lady at church, just casually, if I look alright.

This has been going on for… I’d say several months now, maybe longer; it’s hard to keep track. I find myself checking in the bathroom mirror many times a day, or sometimes avoiding it because I get upset. I know it sounds silly at my age, but I can’t shake the feeling that something is wrong with how I look, like there’s some defect that other people notice but won’t admit. It’s starting to make me more self-conscious about going out.
D017-D005_h024.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Body Dysmorphic Disorder
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Schizophrenia
D017-D005_h024.answer: B & D. Body Dysmorphic Disorder & Schizophrenia

D017-D005_h025.question:
I’ve been really hung up on how my face looks, especially the last 6–7 months. It started as just noticing little things in the mirror, but now I can’t stop checking. When I’m getting ready for a shift, I’ll stand there tilting my head, trying to see if one side of my jaw or my eyes are off. It feels like my whole face is crooked, like people must see it right away.

At the station, I’ll ask the guys, “Does my face look weird to you? Is my nose off-center?” I do that with my wife too. She keeps saying she doesn’t see anything wrong, but I can’t shake the feeling there’s something seriously wrong with how I’m built, like a defect everyone is too polite to point out. Sometimes I catch a glimpse of myself in a window on a call and it throws me off, like I’m looking at a distorted version of me.

I know it sounds odd, and part of me realizes I might be overreacting, but another part is convinced there’s something fundamentally off about how my face is put together.
D017-D005_h025.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Body Dysmorphic Disorder
    C. Adjustment Disorder
    D. Schizophrenia
D017-D005_h025.answer: B & D. Body Dysmorphic Disorder & Schizophrenia
